[[Evanston, Illinois]] (1943–1944) | previous_locations = | years = 1934–1976 | previous_tie-ins = | conference_tie-ins = | payout = | sponsors = ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' | former_names = }} The '''Chicago Charities College All-Star Game''' was a [[preseason]] [[American football]] game played from 1934 to 1976 between the [[National Football League]] (NFL) champions and a team of star [[college football|college]] seniors from the previous year. It was also known as the '''College All-Star Football Classic'''.{{cite journal |last=Grogan |first=John |title=The College All-Star Football Classic |journal=The Coffin Corner |year=2000 |volume=22 |issue=2 |url=http://www.profootballresearchers.org/Coffin_Corner/22-02-841.pdf |access-date=January 30, 2012 |publisher=[[Professional Football Researchers Association]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101218181543/http://profootballresearchers.org/Coffin_Corner/22-02-841.pdf |archive-date=December 18, 2010 |url-status=dead }} The game was contested annually—except for 1974, due to that year's [[1974 NFL strike|NFL strike]]—and was played in July, August, or September. In the 42 College All-Star Games, the defending pro champions won 31, the All-Stars won nine, and two were ties, giving the collegians a .238 winning percentage. The second game, played in 1935, involved the hometown [[1935 Chicago Bears season|Chicago Bears]], runner-up of the [[1934 NFL season|1934 season]], instead of the defending champion [[1935 New York Giants season|New York Giants]]. The [[1969 New York Jets season|New York Jets]] played in the 1969 edition, although still an [[American Football League]] (AFL) team. Once the AFL–NFL Championship was introduced (including for the two seasons before the "[[Super Bowl]]" designation was officially adopted and the remaining two seasons before the [[AFL–NFL merger]]) the Super Bowl winner was the professional team involved, regardless of which league the team represented. ==History of the game== ===Origins=== The game was the idea of [[Arch Ward]], the sports editor of the ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' and the driving force behind [[Major League Baseball]]'s [[Major League Baseball All-Star Game|All-Star Game]]. The game originally was a benefit for [[Chicago]]-area charities and was played at [[Soldier Field]] except for two years during [[World War II]], in 1943 and 1944, when it was held at [[Northwestern University]]'s [[Dyche Stadium]] in [[Evanston, Illinois|Evanston]]. Since Dyche Stadium was smaller than Soldier Field, the wartime federal government ordered the venue switch to reduce attendance and by extension the use of fuel and tires for travel.{{cite book|last=Algeo|first=Matthew|date=September 1, 2013|title=Last Team Standing: How the Steelers and the Eagles—"The Steagles"—Saved Pro Football During World War II|publisher=[[Chicago Review Press]]|isbn=9781613748886|page=21}} The Chicago game was one of several "pro vs. rookie" college all-star games held across the United States in its early years (the [[1939 NFL season|1939 season]] featured seven such games, all of which the NFL teams won in shutouts, and the [[1938 NFL season|season prior]] featured eight, with some of the collegiate players playing in multiple games). Chicago's game had the benefit of being the highest profile, with the NFL champions facing the best college graduates from across the country as opposed to the regional games that were held elsewhere; because of this, the game survived far longer than its contemporaries. [[File:1935 All-Star Collegiate Football (1989.222).jpg|thumb|right|A football signed by the members of the 1935 Collegiate All-Star Team, including [[Gerald Ford]].]] The inaugural game in 1934, played before a crowd of 79,432 on August 31, was a scoreless tie between the All-Stars and the [[1935 Chicago Bears season|Chicago Bears]]. The following year, in a game that included [[Michigan Wolverines football|University of Michigan]] graduate and future [[President of the United States|U.S. president]] [[Gerald Ford]], the Bears won 5–0. ===Highlights=== The first All-Star team to win was the 1937 squad, coached by [[Gus Dorais]], which won 6–0 over [[Curly Lambeau]]'s [[1937 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]]. The only score came on a 47-yard touchdown pass from future [[Pro Football Hall of Fame|Hall of Famer]] [[Sammy Baugh]] to [[Gaynell Tinsley]].{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=AapQAAAAIBAJ&sjid=CiIEAAAAIBAJ&pg=6639%2C6109944 |newspaper=Milwaukee Journal |last=Kuechle |first=Oliver E. |title=Sam Baugh's pass, stalwart defense give Stars 6-0 victory over Packers |date=September 2, 1937|page=5-part 2}} Baugh's [[1938 Washington Redskins season|Washington Redskins]] lost to the All-Stars the next year, but he did not play due to injury.{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=87BQAAAAIBAJ&sjid=EiIEAAAAIBAJ&pg=6582%2C2016183|newspaper=Milwaukee Journal |title=Isbell sparks rally as All-Stars beat Redskins in second half |date=September 1, 1938|page=6-part 2 }} In the 1940s, the games were competitive affairs that attracted large crowds to Soldier Field. The college All-Stars had the benefit of being fully integrated, since the NFL's league-wide color barrier did not apply to the squad, meaning [[black players in American professional football|black players]] such as [[Kenny Washington (American football)|Kenny Washington]] (who played in the 1940 contest) were allowed to play in the game. As the talent level of pro football improved (and the NFL itself integrated), the pros came to dominate the series. The qualifying criteria for the College All-Star squad was loose. The 1945 game featured [[Tom Harmon]], whose professional career had begun in 1941, but had been interrupted by military service.{{cite news|title=Tom Harmon to Join Stars|newspaper=The Milwaukee Journal|date=August 15, 1945|page=10|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1499&dat=19450815&id=EjAaAAAAIBAJ&sjid=ESUEAAAAIBAJ&pg=6460,6313757}} The All-Stars last won consecutive games in 1946 champion, the perennially winning Browns, play that year's game instead of the NFL champion, but after the NFL threatened legal action, the ''Tribune'' board overruled Ward and renewed its agreement with the NFL.The NFL's Official Encyclopedic History of Professional Football, 1977: The AAFC, pgs. 245-251 ===Decline=== [[File:1966-CollegeAllStar-program.jpg|thumb|right|240px|Program for the 1966 game pitting the All-Stars against the World Champion [[Green Bay Packers]].]] By the late 1960s and the 1970s, enthusiasm for the game started to erode as NFL coaches became increasingly reluctant to let their new draftees play in the exhibition game due to their being forced to miss part of training camp, and their draftees being at considerable risk for injury. As early as 1949, these concerns had been raised after [[Dick Rifenburg]] suffered a serious knee injury practicing for the game, effectively ending his professional career before it began, and prompting Rifenburg's move into broadcasting.{{cite news|author=Harmon, Pat|title=''Short-Sighted Pros''|publisher=[[Cedar Rapids Gazette]]|date=1949-08-10}} [[Dan Rooney]], vice president of the Steelers, called the game one that "has turned into a farce" as early as 1970.{{Cite web |date=1970-07-18 |title=Clearfield Progress Archives, Jul 18, 1970, p. 14 |url=https://newspaperarchive.com/clearfield-progress-jul-18-1970-p-14/ |access-date=2026-04-09 |website=NewspaperArchive.com |language=en}} In [[1974 NFL season|1974]], a [[1974 NFL strike|player's strike]] and an exodus of stars to the [[World Football League]] exacerbated this issue, as the NFL went to all-rookie rosters to allow the preseason to be played: with no rookies available to play for the College All-Stars, the [[Canceled NFL games|game was cancelled]] that year. During most of its run, the College All-Star Game was not particularly unique, since NFL teams frequently played exhibition games against non-NFL competition in its early decades. However, by the 1970s, the NFL was withdrawing from competition against teams that were not members of the league. Following the end of preseason games against teams from the [[East Division (CFL)|Eastern Conference]] of the [[Canadian Football League]] in 1961, the NFL played only three games against non-NFL teams (excluding pre-merger exhibition games against AFL teams and College All-Star Games). The first two of these games, a 1969 split-squad match against a [[Continental Football League]] team and a 1972 split-squad match against a [[Seaboard Football League]] team, were large blowout wins for the NFL teams, while the third, between the [[Houston Oilers]] rookie and practice squad and the San Antonio Toros, was a much closer contest. The final College All-Star Game took place in {{nfly|1976}} during a torrential downpour at Soldier Field on July 23.{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=1KtVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=3uADAAAAIBAJ&pg=6480%2C5825113|newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon|agency=Associated Press|title=Rampaging fans, rain shorten all-star game |date=July 24, 1976|page=3B}}{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=NMkbAAAAIBAJ&sjid=vFYEAAAAIBAJ&pg=7035%2C2114956 |work=Pittsburgh Press |last=Sheeley |first=Glenn |title=Splish, splash, Stars take a bath |date=July 24, 1976 |page=6}}{{cite news |url=https://www.si.com/vault/issue/41219/61 |magazine=Sports Illustrated |agency=(photo)|title=A year in sports |date=February 17, 1977 |page=61}} Despite featuring star players such as [[Chuck Muncie]], [[Mike Pruitt]], [[Lee Roy Selmon]], and [[Jackie Slater]], the All-Stars were hopelessly outmatched by the [[1976 Pittsburgh Steelers season|Pittsburgh Steelers]], winners of consecutive Super Bowls ([[Super Bowl IX|IX]], [[Super Bowl X|X]]). The star quarterback for the College All-Stars, Steeler draft pick [[Mike Kruczek]] of [[1975 Boston College Eagles football team|Boston College]], left ten minutes into the first quarter after pulling his left thigh, with backup quarterback [[Craig Penrose]] of [[1975 San Diego State Aztecs football team|San Diego State]] suffering two broken fingers in the second quarter. [[Jeb Blount]] of [[1975 Tulsa Golden Hurricane football team|Tulsa]] played most of the game.{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=NMkbAAAAIBAJ&sjid=vFYEAAAAIBAJ&pg=3368%2C2114435 |work=Pittsburgh Press |last=Sheeley |first=Glenn |title=Noll's view of new faces dampened |date=July 24, 1976 |page=6}} With 1:22 remaining in the third quarter and the Steelers leading 24–0, high winds and lightning prompted All-Stars coach [[Ara Parseghian]] to call for a time out. After the officials ordered both teams to their locker rooms, fans invaded the field and began sliding on the turf as the rain continued to fall heavily. Despite the efforts of officials, stadium security and Chicago Police, all attempts to clear the field failed, with a group of drunk fans tearing down the goalposts at the southern end of the stadium. However, by this time, the torrential rain had left parts of the field under {{convert|18|in|cm|round=0.5}} of water, meaning it would have been unplayable in any event. At 11:01pm [[Central Time Zone|CDT]], NFL Commissioner [[Pete Rozelle]] and the ''Tribune'' announced that the game had been called: the announcement was greeted with jeers, and numerous brawls broke out on the flooded field before order was finally restored. [[Joe Washington]] of [[1975 Oklahoma Sooners football team|Oklahoma]] was selected as the MVP of the final College All-Star game.{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=QvwjAAAAIBAJ&sjid=jH4EAAAAIBAJ&pg=6729%2C1574307 |newspaper=Milwaukee Journal |last=Shepard |first=Terry |title=Rain and fans do in players |date=July 24, 1976 |page=10}} ===Termination and legacy=== Chicago Tribune Charities had every intention of staging a 1977 game, however, a combination of factors, including NFL coaches being increasingly reluctant to let their high draft picks play, rising insurance costs, and higher player salaries meant the game was no longer viable or competitive. As such, the ''Tribune'' announced on December 21, 1976, that the game would be discontinued.{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=_AcqAAAAIBAJ&sjid=OykEAAAAIBAJ&pg=4601%2C905014|newspaper=Milwaukee Journal |title=Game ended by Tribune |date=December 22, 1976|page=10-part 2}}{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=839IAAAAIBAJ&sjid=Tm0DAAAAIBAJ&pg=6921%2C2579194 |work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |title=Chicago Charities withdraw from Star game |date=December 22, 1976 |page=17}}{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=D_xXAAAAIBAJ&sjid=3fYDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6619%2C5938628 |work=The Bulletin |location=Bend, Oregon |agency=Associated Press |title=All-Star tilt choked by rising costs |date=December 22, 1976 |page=15}} The game raised over $4 million for charity during the course of its 42-game run.{{cite news|title=College All-Star Game: A Charity Dies|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=5OMLAAAAIBAJ&sjid=jVgDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6609,1573517&hl=en|access-date=January 30, 2012|newspaper=[[Evening Independent]]|date=December 22, 1967|agency=[[Chicago Tribune]]|page=1-C}} In the 42 College All-Star Games, the defending pro champions won 31, the All-Stars won nine, and two were ties, giving the collegians a {{winning percentage|9|31|2}} winning percentage. The 1976 College All-Star Game remains, as of 2025, the last time an NFL team has played any team from outside the league. One aspect of the College All-Star Game was later revived: the concept of the league champion playing in the first game of the season was adopted in [[2004 NFL season|2004]] with the [[National Football League Kickoff game]]. Since then, the first game of the regular season is hosted by the defending Super Bowl champion. ==Game results== All games played at [[Soldier Field]] in [[Chicago]], except for the 1943 and 1944
